report_unavailable_tool: web — I cannot access the web or current guideline documents right now, so I cannot retrieve or cite current pediatric guidelines.

I cannot give a definite diagnosis from this chat. With a child who has a spreading rash plus fever and unknown duration, I can only give safety-focused, generally accepted triage steps you should follow tonight:

1) Go to emergency care now or call emergency services if your child has any of:
   - Difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, or blue lips/face
   - Swelling of the face or tongue or sudden hoarseness
   - Very drowsy, hard to wake, confused, or unresponsive
   - Repeated vomiting or cannot keep fluids down / signs of dehydration
   - Severe pain or extreme irritability
   - Neck stiffness or severe headache with fever
   - Rash that is rapidly spreading with collapse or fainting, or non‑blanching purple spots/petechiae
   - Very high fever (for example, >104°F/40°C) or fever in a child who is medically fragile/immunocompromised

2) If none of the emergency signs above and the child seems relatively well (alert, drinking fluids, breathing comfortably):
   - Contact your pediatrician, an after‑hours nurse line, or urgent care tonight for advice and possible in‑person evaluation.
   - Keep the child comfortable, encourage fluids, and you may give fever‑reducing medicine per the product labeling or your clinician’s usual instructions for your child’s weight/age.
   - Take clear photos of the rash (good lighting, close and wide shots), note when it started, how it has changed, any new medications, recent illnesses, sick contacts, travel, or insect bites—bring or send those to the clinician.

I cannot cite guideline sources here because I cannot access the web; I also cannot determine a diagnosis without an examination and relevant history/tests. If you want, tell me the child’s current symptoms (appearance of the rash, whether it blanches, location, associated symptoms, temperature reading, any recent meds/exposures) and I can help you prioritize concerns to report when you call a clinician.
